question: What is the main job of sensory nerves in our body?

options.A: Producing hormones to regulate metabolic rate
options.B: Transmitting information from body tissues to the central nervous system
options.C: Carrying signals away from the brain to muscles

explanation: Spot on! Sensory nerves act like telephone wires, carrying messages from your skin and organs back to the brain and spinal cord so you know what's happening around you. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h1)

question: Which part of the nervous system includes the sensory nerves branching out to your skin and organs?
explanation: You got it! Think of the central nervous system as the main office (brain and spinal cord), while the peripheral nervous system is the field crew reaching out to every corner of the body. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h1)

question: Where do you usually find the cell bodies of most sensory neurons?

options.D: Anterior horns of the spinal cord

explanation: Well done! Sensory neuron cell bodies neatly cluster together in little swellings called dorsal root ganglia right outside the spinal cord. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h2)

question: How are typical primary sensory neurons classified based on their structure?
explanation: Correct! Most sensory neurons are unipolar, meaning they have a single main branch that splits into two directions—one toward the body and one toward the spinal cord. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h2)

question: Which type of nerve receptor is mainly responsible for detecting tissue damage or pain?
explanation: Spot on! Nociceptors are your body's early warning alarm system. They fire up when tissues experience actual or potential damage, creating the feeling of pain. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h3)

question: A patient touches a hot stove and quickly pulls their hand away. Which receptors flagged this danger?
explanation: Brilliant! Thermoreceptors felt the intense heat, and nociceptors screamed 'ouch!'—triggering that fast reflex to protect the hand. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h3)

question: What is the main goal of sensory transduction?

options.B: Releasing digestive enzymes into the bloodstream
options.C: Converting environmental stimuli into electrical signals
options.D: Storing memories within the cerebral cortex

explanation: You nailed it! Transduction is simply the nervous system's translator, turning physical sensations like touch or light into electrical language the brain can understand. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h4)

question: What local voltage change happens in a sensory receptor before an action potential fires?
explanation: Correct! When a stimulus hits a receptor, it causes a small local voltage shift called a receptor or generator potential before sending a full signal down the nerve. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h4)

question: Which brain structure acts as the main relay station for incoming sensory messages before they reach the cortex?
explanation: Spot on! The thalamus is like a busy airport control tower, sorting and routing almost all incoming sensory signals to the correct spots in the brain. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h5)

question: What do second-order neurons typically do in ascending sensory pathways?

options.A: They secrete neurotransmitters onto sweat glands
options.B: They directly connect skin receptors to motor neurons
options.C: They cross the midline and ascend to the thalamus
options.D: They store long-term sensory memories in the frontal lobe

explanation: You got it! Second-order neurons cross over (decussate) to the opposite side of the spinal cord or brainstem before heading up to the thalamus. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h5)

question: In which lobe of the brain is the primary somatosensory cortex found?
explanation: Great job! The primary somatosensory cortex lives right in the parietal lobe, processing all your touches, temperatures, and body positions. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h6)

question: Why do our hands and face get a much larger area on the sensory homunculus than our back or thighs?

options.A: They are closer physically to the brain
options.B: They contain larger bones and thicker muscles
options.C: They receive more blood flow from the carotid arteries
options.D: They have a much higher density of sensory receptors

explanation: Spot on! Areas of the body we use for fine, detailed feeling (like fingertips and lips) have way more receptors, so the brain gives them extra processing space. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h6)

question: A nurse wants to check a patient's light touch feeling on their legs. What is the best tool to use?

options.A: A cold metal stethoscope bell pressed firmly
options.B: A wisp of cotton stroked lightly over the skin
options.C: A sterile needle poked deep into the muscle
options.D: A low-frequency tuning fork on the patella

explanation: Correct! Gently brushing a cotton wisp across the skin is a classic, gentle way to test light touch pathways without causing discomfort. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h7)

question: Why do we ask a patient to close their eyes during a sensory nerve physical examination?

options.A: To relax the autonomic nervous system and lower blood pressure
options.B: To prevent accidental corneal injury from reflex movements
options.C: To prevent visual compensation and ensure accurate sensory testing
options.D: To enhance the patient's hearing during verbal instructions

explanation: You nailed it! Closing the eyes stops patients from cheating by looking at where you touch them, giving you a true test of their nerve pathways. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T28#GNS211_U3_T28_h7)
